title: 2027-09-21 Verdant AI POC Scoping — Latency SLOs
summary: POC scoping focused on defining latency and throughput SLOs (TTFT vs TPOT), workload sizing, and a measurement plan. Agreed to a 3-week POC with baseline microbenchmarks, production-replay, and weekly checkpoints. Redwood to share benchmark configs, draft test plan, and security docs. Customer cares about p95/p99 targets and warm vs cold cache behavior.
action_items: Maya Chen: Share benchmark harness repo and example config (due 2027-09-23)
Rafael Ortiz: Prepare initial microbenchmark config for 2 model variants (due 2027-09-24)
Priya Nair: Provide 1 week of request traces and sample prompts (due 2027-09-24)
Sara Gomez: Open network/peering questions and provide account infra details (due 2027-09-24)
next_steps: Redwood to run baseline microbenchmarks (TTFT/TPOT) and share results
Customer to provide anonymized production traces and target traffic profile
Schedule 60m benchmark run in Redwood staging (week 2)
Finalize POC success criteria doc and sign-off
transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Today is the POC scoping for latency SLOs — focusing on TTFT vs TPOT and how we'll measure p95/p99. We got about 50 minutes, is that still good?
[00:08] Priya (Verdant): Yep, that's great. We have Liam and Sara on from infra as well.
[00:12] Liam (Verdant): Morning—afternoon—yeah, thanks. We want to make sure the POC proves we can meet production latency SLOs before committing to dedicated capacity.
[00:20] Rafael (Redwood SE): Totally, and we'll scope both synthetic microbenchmarks and a production replay to capture tail behavior. Quick question on definitions: when we say TTFT some people call that time-to-first-token or first-byte; others use cold-start vs warm. We're going to use TTFT = time from request accept to first token generated by the model, and TPOT = time per output token once streaming begins.
[00:40] Priya: Good, clarify that now. For us p95 TTFT matters a lot for interactive features; p99 is also important but we'll tolerate a few high tails if throughput is good.
[00:52] Ethan (Redwood): Helpful to quantify — what are your current targets or expectations?
[00:56] Priya: We're aiming for p95 TTFT <= 250ms for a 32-token response and TPOT p95 <= 12ms per token. p99 goals are a bit looser — p99 TTFT <= 600ms, TPOT p99 <= 30ms. Those are aspirational but will be our success criteria if feasible.
[01:14] Rafael: That's a useful starting point. We'll test with two model variants: a smaller open LLM (quantized) and the midsize variant you mentioned in the questionnaire. We'll capture both cold and warm cache behavior — cold meaning new model process or cold KV cache, warm meaning steady-state with KV/prefix cache warm.
[01:32] Sara (Verdant): For the infra side, we're curious about the measurement signals — do you record first-byte times and per-token timing on Redwood's dashboard?
[01:40] Maya: Yes, Redwood Console surfaces token-level timings, TTFT, per-token latency (TPOT), and token counts. We also provide traces and raw logs you can ingest into your observability stack. small disclaimer — sometimes the telemetry labels get slightly garbled in the transcript, we try to keep consistent naming though.
[01:55] Noah (Verdant): One of our big concerns is that our workload is bursty — daytime spikes up to 600 qps and quieter nights. How does that map to POC sizing?
[02:04] Rafael: For the POC we'll define two load profiles: low steady (50 qps), medium (200 qps), and a short burst to simulate peak (600 qps) for 2-3 minutes. We'll run each profile for enough time to stabilize metrics — e.g., 10 minutes for steady, and a 5-10 minute poison for burst.
[02:22] Priya: That sounds right. How will you measure p95/p99 under burst? I assume you run concurrent clients with realistic prompt lengths?
[02:30] Ethan: Exactly. We'll replay anonymized request traces you provide plus synthetic variations to capture token length distribution. We'll also vary concurrency to stress the KV/cache and batching.
[02:38] Liam: Another point — we need to understand the impact of quantization and batching on both TTFT and TPOT. We don't want an optimization that reduces cost but kills the user experience with higher first token latency.
[02:49] Rafael: Agreed. Our plan is to run each model variant under two runtime configs: full precision (FP16) and a quantized profile you may use in production. We'll also sweep batching window sizes and batch size caps to find an operating point that balances TTFT and TPOT.
[03:03] Priya: Can you give an example of how batching affects TTFT? I always thought batching helps throughput but hurts latency.
[03:10] Rafael: Right — batching increases per-request wait for the first token because you may hold a request for batching window. But continuous batching with small windows plus prefix/KV caching can keep TTFT low while improving throughput. Example: at 100 qps a small 10ms batching window might add ~5-15ms to TTFT but reduce TPOT by 20-40% in some cases.
[03:29] Maya: We'll include those sweep results in the deliverable. Now on measurements — we plan two phases: Phase A microbenchmarks (TTFT/TPOT on contrived short prompts, controlled concurrency) and Phase B production replay (using your traces, end-to-end latency including network).
[03:45] Priya: For Phase B, we need to make sure the replay keeps the temporal pattern; otherwise tails are not realistic.
[03:50] Rafael: We'll do both a time-dependent replay (same timestamps relative to a scaled timeline) and a randomized shuffle to stress tails. We'll also do cold-start runs where we restart the model instances to measure cold TTFT.
[04:03] Noah: About telemetry — can Redwood attach request ids so we can correlate with our logs? That's essential for debugging p99 events.
[04:09] Maya: Yes -- we'll include a request-id header and full trace ids that you can correlate. We'll also ship CSVs that include timestamp, request-id, model-variant, TTFT, TPOT per token, token counts, and GPU utilization samples.
[04:23] Liam: Great. What about measurement windows for p95/p99? Do you compute over sliding windows or across the entire run?
[04:29] Rafael: We'll provide both: sliding 5-minute windows to show stability and the aggregated p95/p99 over the steady-state period. For burst, we'll report tail percentiles during the burst window separately.
[04:39] Priya: Let's talk success criteria and go/no-go. Our internal bar is: p95 TTFT <= 250ms at medium load (200 qps) for 32-token responses, and TPOT p95 <= 12ms. p99 TTFT <= 600ms but if p99 is worse than that we need to see mitigation plans.
[04:56] Maya: Redwood proposed a Go/No-Go rubric in the questionnaire: Green if both p95 and p99 meet targets for medium load and burst does not exceed x% error rate; Yellow if p95 meets but p99 misses by under 2x; Red if p95 misses. We'll formalize that in the POC success doc.
[05:09] Sara: Also need to include reliability metrics — error rate, API throttles, and cold-start frequency.
[05:15] Ethan: We'll include those as secondary success metrics and collect server-side traces for any 500/502-style errors.
[05:22] Priya: What's the POC timeline look like? We indicated 3 weeks in the questionnaire.
[05:26] Maya: Proposed schedule: Week 0 (kickoff, data exchange), Week 1 (Phase A: microbenchmarks + tuning), Week 2 (Phase B: production replay + tuning), Week 3 (final run, results, and handoff). We'll leave room for one extra week if we need deeper infra work.
[05:40] Liam: Who's owning each milestone?
[05:43] Maya: Redwood will own running benchmarks and delivering reports; Verdant provides traces and infra access details; mutual weekly check-ins with AE/SE and customer leads. We'll add concrete owners in the POC doc.
[05:54] Priya: On the measurement plan specifics — tokenization differences can skew TPOT. We tokenize differently across models; can you guarantee consistent token counts?
[06:02] Rafael: We'll run exact tokenizer parity tests: same tokenizer binary and config. If you have custom tokenizers or prompt templating that changes token counts, please provide examples. We'll normalize results to per-token metrics and also include per-character or per-word counts if helpful.
[06:17] Noah: For network, we need to know region and egress patterns. We'll try staging in us-west-2 to match production.
[06:23] Ethan: Redwood can run benchmark clusters in us-west-2 staging. We'll also measure RTT separately by adding synthetic network delay to isolate network impact vs model inference.
[06:34] Priya: Regarding tooling — will you share the harness so we can reproduce runs in our environment?
[06:39] Rafael: Yes, we'll share a reproducible harness on Git. It uses k6 for traffic generation and a small Python runner that records per-token timings using the streaming API. You can run it locally or point it at Redwood staging.
[06:52] Maya: On security/compliance, we'll send the SOC2 summary and the private deployment checklist. You asked about whether logs contain customer data — by default we mask request bodies for hosted POC but we can enable private plane options or provide a private deployment for more sensitive content.
[07:06] Sara: We will probably want masked logs for the hosted run, but we'll also explore a VPC option if the POC shows promising results.
[07:13] Priya: One more question — for TPOT how do you measure when streaming vs non-streaming models?
[07:19] Rafael: For streaming we measure inter-token intervals after first token. For non-streaming we compute time-from-first-byte to last-byte divided by token count to get average per-token; we also report distribution across tokens since some implementations produce variable token timing.
[07:34] Priya: Okay. Are you going to include GPU utilization and KV cache hit rates in the report?
[07:38] Ethan: Yes we'll include GPU metrics (util, mem) and runtime stats including KV cache hit/miss, batch sizes, and queueing delays. That helps explain why tails happen.
[07:48] Maya: Let's capture the concrete POC success criteria now for the doc: 1) p95 TTFT <= 250ms at medium load (200 qps) for 32-token responses. 2) p95 TPOT <= 12ms. 3) p99 TTFT <= 600ms or a documented mitigation plan. 4) Error rate < 0.5% during steady-state. 5) No single-mode cold start events causing >2x of baseline during final run.
[08:13] Priya: That looks good. Can you also include optional cost targets? We want to understand cost per 1k queries at the operating point.
[08:20] Maya: We'll estimate cost based on the recommended config and batch settings; we'll include a per-1k-requests cost estimate in the final deck.
[08:27] Liam: For the microbench specifics — what's your recommended run length to get stable p99 estimates? We know p99 needs lots of samples.
[08:34] Rafael: For p99 we aim for at least 1M requests total for a stable estimate, but that's not always feasible. Practically, we'll run longer steady-state windows (30-60 minutes) or multiple runs aggregated to get better tails. If you can't run that long, we'll use bootstrapped confidence intervals and indicate uncertainty.
[08:50] Priya: Understood. For the POC we'll try to provide enough budget/time for a 30-minute steady-state at medium load.
[08:57] Sara: Network egress — we will enable peering with the Redwood staging account; I'll send the peering request details.
[09:02] Maya: Perfect. I'll add that as an action item. Rafael, anything else on the measurement plan?
[09:08] Rafael: One more thing — we recommend measuring TTFT against cold-process starts (container spin up) and cold-kv cache separately. Those have different remediation strategies: warm pools vs persistent processes vs caching. We'll document both.
[09:23] Priya: If you can show both numbers it's helpful. Also include the precise input distribution (token lengths percentiles) in the report.
[09:29] Maya: We'll include a target input distribution table and use it to generate synthetic prompts.
[09:34] Liam: Last question — what's the engineered fallback plan if the SLOs aren't met in production? Is Redwood able to route to a smaller/larger model or to a different region?
[09:43] Ethan: Yes — Redwood supports smart routing and automatic fallback to lower-cost or higher-latency variants; in enterprise we can configure policy-based routing by latency or cost, and have canary rollouts. We'll include a demo of fallback logic in the post-POC handoff.
[09:58] Maya: Ok let's recap next steps quickly. Action items I captured earlier. We'll run Phase A microbench next week once we get traces and the config. Redwood will share the harness and initial results within 48-72 hours of starting the runs.
[10:12] Priya: Thanks, that timeline works. Anything else?
[10:15] Noah: No, thanks everyone.
[10:17] Maya: Great, we'll follow up with calendar invites for the weekly checkpoints and share the POC doc. Thanks all.
[10:22] End of transcript.

Notes on transcript quality: occasional mis-attribution, some acronyms parsed as individual letters (e.g., T T F T), and minor filler words.

POC Measurement Plan (short bullets captured live):
- Phase A: Microbenchmarks
  - Measure TTFT and TPOT for 2 model variants (FP16 and quantized).
  - Controlled concurrency: 50 qps, 200 qps, burst 600 qps (2-3 min).
  - Run batching window sweeps (5ms, 10ms, 20ms) and batch size caps.
  - Cold start vs warm cache runs.
  - Capture GPU util, mem, KV cache hit/miss, queueing delays.
- Phase B: Production Replay
  - Use anonymized traces from Verdant (Priya to provide).
  - Time-preserving replay + randomized shuffle.
  - 30 minute steady-state at medium load for p99 estimation; aggregate runs for confidence intervals.
  - Correlate request-ids with Verdant logs for p99 debugging.
- Metrics and Reporting
  - TTFT p50/p95/p99, TPOT p50/p95/p99, error rates, throughput (qps), GPU util, KV cache hit rate.
  - Sliding 5-minute windows + aggregated steady-state percentiles.
  - CSV deliverable with per-request fields: timestamp, request-id, model, variant, TTFT_ms, TPOT_ms_avg, token_count, batch_size, gpu_util_pct.
- Success Criteria (Draft)
  - p95 TTFT <= 250ms at 200 qps for 32-token responses.
  - p95 TPOT <= 12ms.
  - p99 TTFT <= 600ms or documented mitigation.
  - Error rate < 0.5% steady-state.
  - No repeated cold-start events during final run.

POC Timeline (draft):
- Week 0: Kickoff, data exchange, harness config (this week).
- Week 1: Phase A microbenchmarks + tuning.
- Week 2: Phase B production replay + tuning.
- Week 3: Final run, handoff, cost estimate, and postmortem.

Deliverables Redwood will provide:
- Benchmark harness (Git repo) and example configs.
- Baseline microbenchmark report (TTFT/TPOT per model/variant).
- Production replay report and CSVs.
- POC success criteria doc and go/no-go rubric.
- Security docs (SOC2 summary, private deployment checklist).
